claim: Chronic high-fat feeding triggers metabolic dysfunction including obesity, insulin resistance, and diabetes.
source: Chronic high-fat feeding triggers metabolic dysfunction including obesity, insulin resistance, and diabetes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the effects of chronic high-fat feeding.

claim: High-fat intake rapidly increases palmitate levels in cerebrospinal fluid.
source: High-fat intake rapidly increases palmitate levels in cerebrospinal fluid and triggers a wave of microglial metabolic activation characterized by mitochondrial membrane activation and fission as well as metabolic skewing toward aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CSF metabolomics presented in the manuscript.

claim: High-fat intake triggers a wave of microglial metabolic activation characterized by mitochondrial membrane activation and fission.
source: High-fat intake rapidly increases palmitate levels in cerebrospinal fluid and triggers a wave of microglial metabolic activation characterized by mitochondrial membrane activation and fission as well as metabolic skewing toward aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of mitochondrial membrane potential and morphology.

claim: High-fat intake triggers metabolic skewing toward aerobic glycolysis in microglia.
source: High-fat intake rapidly increases palmitate levels in cerebrospinal fluid and triggers a wave of microglial metabolic activation characterized by mitochondrial membrane activation and fission as well as metabolic skewing toward aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing experiments showing increased lactate production.

claim: The microglial metabolic response to HFD is detectable within as little as 12 hr of HFD exposure.
source: These effects are detectable throughout the brain and can be detected within as little as 12 hr of HFD exposure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing mitochondrial membrane potential changes at 12 hr.

claim: Microglial ablation shows that the microglial metabolic response is necessary for the acute effects of HFD.
source: In vivo, microglial ablation and conditional DRP1 deletion show that the microglial metabolic response is necessary for the acute effects of HFD.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using PLX5622 to deplete microglia.

claim: Conditional DRP1 deletion shows that the microglial metabolic response is necessary for the acute effects of HFD.
source: In vivo, microglial ablation and conditional DRP1 deletion show that the microglial metabolic response is necessary for the acute effects of HFD.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using Drp1MGKO mice.

claim: Microglia process palmitate via β-oxidation.
source: 13C-tracing experiments reveal that in addition to processing via β-oxidation, microglia shunt a substantial fraction of palmitate toward anaplerosis and re-release of bioenergetic carbons into the extracellular milieu in the form of lactate, glutamate, succinate, and intriguingly, the neuroprotective metabolite itaconate.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-palmitate tracing experiments showing labeled acetylcarnitine and TCA intermediates.

claim: Microglia shunt a substantial fraction of palmitate toward anaplerosis.
source: 13C-tracing experiments reveal that in addition to processing via β-oxidation, microglia shunt a substantial fraction of palmitate toward anaplerosis and re-release of bioenergetic carbons into the extracellular milieu in the form of lactate, glutamate, succinate, and intriguingly, the neuroprotective metabolite itaconate.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing data showing labeled glutamate and other metabolites.

claim: Microglia re-release bioenergetic carbons into the extracellular milieu in the form of lactate, glutamate, succinate, and itaconate.
source: 13C-tracing experiments reveal that in addition to processing via β-oxidation, microglia shunt a substantial fraction of palmitate toward anaplerosis and re-release of bioenergetic carbons into the extracellular milieu in the form of lactate, glutamate, succinate, and intriguingly, the neuroprotective metabolite itaconate.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing experiments measuring labeled metabolites in extracellular media.

claim: Itaconate is a neuroprotective metabolite.
source: 13C-tracing experiments reveal that in addition to processing via β-oxidation, microglia shunt a substantial fraction of palmitate toward anaplerosis and re-release of bioenergetic carbons into the extracellular milieu in the form of lactate, glutamate, succinate, and intriguingly, the neuroprotective metabolite itaconate.
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on itaconate's neuroprotective properties.

claim: Microglia are a critical nutrient regulatory node in the brain, metabolizing away harmful fatty acids and liberating the same carbons as alternate bioenergetic and protective substrates for surrounding cells.
source: Together, these data identify microglia as a critical nutrient regulatory node in the brain, metabolizing away harmful fatty acids and liberating the same carbons as alternate bioenergetic and protective substrates for surrounding cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing fatty acid uptake and metabolite release.

claim: Short-term HFD has a surprisingly beneficial effect on learning and memory.
source: The data identify a surprisingly beneficial effect of short-term HFD on learning and memory.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data showing improved performance in Barnes and T-Maze tests.

claim: The central nervous system plays a critical role in regulating glucose and energy homeostasis by sensing, integrating, and responding to peripheral signals.
source: The central nervous system (CNS) plays a critical role in regulating glucose and energy homeostasis by sensing, integrating, and responding to peripheral signals (Kleinridders et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Understanding of CNS control over energy balance is mostly derived from investigation of distinct functional sets of hypothalamic neurons and their interactions with the periphery.
source: Our understanding of CNS control over energy balance is mostly derived from investigation of distinct functional sets of hypothalamic neurons and their interactions with the periphery (Grayson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A growing body of evidence supports an important role for glial cells in regulating energy balance.
source: In addition, a growing body of evidence supports an important role for glial cells in regulating energy balance (Argente-Arizón et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Astrocytes can regulate energy balance by processing glucose into lactate, which is then released to fuel and modulate surrounding neurons.
source: For example, astrocytes can regulate energy balance by processing glucose into lactate, which is then released to fuel and modulate surrounding neurons (Pellerin et al., 1998; Magistretti and Allaman, 2018; Bélanger et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Metabolic intermediaries from the neuronal niche can directly influence CNS output.
source: These latter findings demonstrate how metabolic intermediaries from the neuronal niche can directly influence CNS output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited astrocyte-lactate literature.

claim: Microglia are the third most abundant glial cell in the brain.
source: Microglia are the third most abundant glial cell in the brain.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about microglial abundance.

claim: Microglia are derived from the yolk sac developmentally.
source: Developmentally, they are derived from the yolk sac and are considered CNS immune cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about microglial development.

claim: Microglia are considered CNS immune cells.
source: Developmentally, they are derived from the yolk sac and are considered CNS immune cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about microglial function.

claim: Microglial activation has been implicated in metabolic disease pathogenesis.
source: Like the peripheral immune compartment, microglial activation has been implicated in metabolic disease pathogenesis (Thaler et al., 2012; Valdearcos et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglia in the mediobasal hypothalamus become activated under conditions of chronic high-fat feeding in a process termed 'microgliosis'.
source: Specifically, microglia in the mediobasal hypothalamus (MBH) become activated under conditions of chronic high-fat feeding in a process termed 'microgliosis'.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HFD-induced microglial activation has been associated with moderate increases in cytokine gene expression.
source: High-fat diet (HFD)-induced activation has been associated with moderate increases in cytokine gene expression (Thaler et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2017) and pioneering studies testing both genetic manipulation of microglial NF-kB and microglial depletion with PLX5622 suggest that microglial activation is necessary for the metabolic impairments triggered by chronic HFD (Valdearcos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Genetic manipulation of microglial NF-kB and microglial depletion with PLX5622 suggest that microglial activation is necessary for the metabolic impairments triggered by chronic HFD.
source: High-fat diet (HFD)-induced activation has been associated with moderate increases in cytokine gene expression (Thaler et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2017) and pioneering studies testing both genetic manipulation of microglial NF-kB and microglial depletion with PLX5622 suggest that microglial activation is necessary for the metabolic impairments triggered by chronic HFD (Valdearcos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Recent evidence suggests a role for microglial mitochondrial alterations (fission) that can be detected within days of HFD administration.
source: Recent evidence suggests a role for microglial mitochondrial alterations (fission) that can be detected within days of HFD administration (Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Microglia outside the hypothalamus also activate upon chronic HFD exposure.
source: Microglia outside the hypothalamus also activate upon chronic HFD exposure (Vinuesa et al., 2019; Hao et al., 2016) and associate with cognitive impairment (Spencer et al., 2017; Duffy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglial activation upon chronic HFD exposure associates with cognitive impairment.
source: Microglia outside the hypothalamus also activate upon chronic HFD exposure (Vinuesa et al., 2019; Hao et al., 2016) and associate with cognitive impairment (Spencer et al., 2017; Duffy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglia respond to dietary fat within a single 12 hr feeding cycle.
source: Here, we find that microglia respond to dietary fat within single 12 hr feeding cycle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing mitochondrial changes at 12 hr.

claim: By 3 days, HFD increases microglial mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: By 3 days, HFD increases microglial mitochondrial membrane potential, inhibits complex II activity, and skews mitochondria toward fission.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using MitoTracker staining.

claim: By 3 days, HFD inhibits microglial complex II activity.
source: By 3 days, HFD increases microglial mitochondrial membrane potential, inhibits complex II activity, and skews mitochondria toward fission.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using Seahorse and TMRM assays.

claim: By 3 days, HFD skews microglia mitochondria toward fission.
source: By 3 days, HFD increases microglial mitochondrial membrane potential, inhibits complex II activity, and skews mitochondria toward fission.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing mitochondrial morphology changes.

claim: Microglia are directly exposed to increased palmitate and stearate levels within hours of the feeding switch.
source: Using cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metabolomics we demonstrate that microglia are directly exposed to increased palmitate and stearate levels within hours of the feeding switch, and using 13C-tracer studies, we find that microglia robustly metabolize fatty acids via β-oxidation.
evidence: This is supported by CSF metabolomics data.

claim: Microglia robustly metabolize fatty acids via β-oxidation.
source: Using cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metabolomics we demonstrate that microglia are directly exposed to increased palmitate and stearate levels within hours of the feeding switch, and using 13C-tracer studies, we find that microglia robustly metabolize fatty acids via β-oxidation.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-palmitate tracing experiments.

claim: The acute microglial metabolic response (aMMR) occurs beyond the hypothalamus in vivo, in the hippocampus and cortex.
source: Interestingly, we find the same acute microglial metabolic response (aMMR) beyond the hypothalamus in vivo, in the hippocampus and cortex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing mitochondrial membrane potential changes in cortical and hippocampal microglia.

claim: aMMR is largely independent of transcriptional changes.
source: aMMR is largely independent of transcriptional changes, and intriguingly, we find that it improves spatial and learning memory.
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data showing no significant transcriptional changes.

claim: aMMR improves spatial and learning memory.
source: aMMR is largely independent of transcriptional changes, and intriguingly, we find that it improves spatial and learning memory.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data (Barnes test, T-Maze).

claim: Microglia are necessary for the immediate whole-body glucose homeostatic response to acute HFD.
source: Microglial depletion experiments and microglia-specific DRP deletion show that microglia and more specifically microglial mitochondrial fission are necessary for both the immediate whole-body glucose homeostatic response and the memory improvements to acute HFD.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using PLX5622 and Drp1MGKO mice.

claim: Microglial mitochondrial fission is necessary for the immediate whole-body glucose homeostatic response to acute HFD.
source: Microglial depletion experiments and microglia-specific DRP deletion show that microglia and more specifically microglial mitochondrial fission are necessary for both the immediate whole-body glucose homeostatic response and the memory improvements to acute HFD.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using Drp1MGKO mice.

claim: Microglia are necessary for the memory improvements to acute HFD.
source: Microglial depletion experiments and microglia-specific DRP deletion show that microglia and more specifically microglial mitochondrial fission are necessary for both the immediate whole-body glucose homeostatic response and the memory improvements to acute HFD.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tests in PLX5622-treated mice.

claim: Microglial mitochondrial fission is necessary for the memory improvements to acute HFD.
source: Microglial depletion experiments and microglia-specific DRP deletion show that microglia and more specifically microglial mitochondrial fission are necessary for both the immediate whole-body glucose homeostatic response and the memory improvements to acute HFD.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tests in Drp1MGKO mice.

claim: The data identify a non-transcriptional microglial metabolic mechanism that links detection of acute changes in dietary fat to changes in whole-body metabolism and memory.
source: The data thus identify a non-transcriptional microglial metabolic mechanism that links detection of acute changes in dietary fat to changes in whole-body metabolism and memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined experimental data.

claim: Metabolically healthy mice exhibit rapid metabolic shifts on a 3-day timescale, including fasting and post-absorptive hyperglycemia.
source: Metabolically healthy mice exhibit rapid metabolic shifts on this timescale, including fasting and post-absorptive (2 hr fast) hyperglycemia and an elevated insulin response to glucose (Figure 1B–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B; Benani et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and cited literature.

claim: Metabolically healthy mice exhibit an elevated insulin response to glucose upon acute HFD.
source: Metabolically healthy mice exhibit rapid metabolic shifts on this timescale, including fasting and post-absorptive (2 hr fast) hyperglycemia and an elevated insulin response to glucose (Figure 1B–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B; Benani et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and cited literature.

claim: Glucose excursion and insulin tolerance were minimally impacted upon acute HFD.
source: Glucose excursion, as revealed by baseline correction, and insulin tolerance were minimally impacted upon acute HFD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), an important contrast to chronic HFD (Gregor and Hotamisligil, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and cited literature.

claim: The acute changes in glycemic control upon HFD are transient, returning to homeostatic levels within 1 week of a return to normal chow.
source: These acute changes in glycemic control were transient, returning to homeostatic levels within 1 week of a return to normal chow ('Reverse Diet'; Figure 1C–E) and are not associated with substantial body weight gain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Acute HFD changes in glycemic control are not associated with substantial body weight gain.
source: These acute changes in glycemic control were transient, returning to homeostatic levels within 1 week of a return to normal chow ('Reverse Diet'; Figure 1C–E) and are not associated with substantial body weight gain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: PLX-5622 treatment depleted hypothalamic microglia by >95% across animals.
source: PLX-5622 treatment depleted hypothalamic microglia by >95% across animals (Figure 1F), without body weight gain or food intake modification (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B) and prevented induction of both the 3d HFD insulin hypersecretion and post-absorptive hyperglycemia (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: PLX-5622 treatment did not cause body weight gain or food intake modification.
source: PLX-5622 treatment depleted hypothalamic microglia by >95% across animals (Figure 1F), without body weight gain or food intake modification (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B) and prevented induction of both the 3d HFD insulin hypersecretion and post-absorptive hyperglycemia (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: PLX-5622 treatment prevented induction of 3d HFD insulin hypersecretion.
source: PLX-5622 treatment depleted hypothalamic microglia by >95% across animals (Figure 1F), without body weight gain or food intake modification (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B) and prevented induction of both the 3d HFD insulin hypersecretion and post-absorptive hyperglycemia (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: PLX-5622 treatment prevented induction of 3d HFD post-absorptive hyperglycemia.
source: PLX-5622 treatment depleted hypothalamic microglia by >95% across animals (Figure 1F), without body weight gain or food intake modification (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B) and prevented induction of both the 3d HFD insulin hypersecretion and post-absorptive hyperglycemia (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Hyperglycemia associated with overnight fasting was unaffected by microglial depletion.
source: Hyperglycemia associated with overnight fasting was unaffected by microglial depletion (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Acute HFD triggers microglia-dependent and independent metabolic effects.
source: The latter indicates that acute HFD triggers microglia-dependent and independent metabolic effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of microglial depletion on fasting vs post-absorptive hyperglycemia.

claim: Microglia are required for metabolic changes induced by the transition to high-fat feeding.
source: Thus, microglia are required for metabolic changes induced by the transition to high-fat feeding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PLX5622 depletion experiments.

claim: Long-term exposure to HFD has been associated with hypothalamic microgliosis and monocyte infiltration.
source: Long-term exposure to HFD has previously been associated with hypothalamic microgliosis (increased number and activation of CD45lo;CD11b+ microglia) and monocyte infiltration (CD45hi;Cd11b+) (Valdearcos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: 3d HFD exposure showed no evidence of increased hypothalamic microglial proliferation.
source: Examination of 3d HFD responses in both wild-type animals and animals harboring a microglia-restricted eYFP lineage reporter showed no evidence of either increased hypothalamic microglial proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) or monocyte infiltration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: 3d HFD exposure showed no evidence of monocyte infiltration.
source: Examination of 3d HFD responses in both wild-type animals and animals harboring a microglia-restricted eYFP lineage reporter showed no evidence of either increased hypothalamic microglial proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) or monocyte infiltration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Using scRNAseq, there was no evidence of a significant microglial transcriptional response to 3d HFD exposure.
source: Similarly, using the highly sensitive single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNAseq) protocols, CEL-Seq2, we found no evidence of a significant microglial transcriptional response to this very short-term HFD exposure.
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data analysis.

claim: The scRNAseq analysis included searches for changes in heterogeneity, skewing across sub-states, and appearance of new cell sub-states.
source: The latter analysis included searches for changes in heterogeneity, skewing across sub-states, and appearance of new cell sub-states (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: The lack of transcriptional response to 3d HFD was especially clear when juxtaposed to experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE)-triggered responses.
source: The lack of response was especially clear when juxtaposed to experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE)-triggered responses performed using the same purification and sequencing protocols in the same laboratory (EAE; Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by comparative scRNAseq data shown in figures.

claim: The central effects of acute HFD are distinct from those of chronic HFD.
source: Thus, the central effects of acute HFD are distinct from those of chronic HFD, and have little to no effect on microglial expansion, transcription, heterogeneity, or inflammation in the hypothalamus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of acute vs chronic HFD effects.

claim: Acute HFD has little to no effect on microglial expansion, transcription, heterogeneity, or inflammation in the hypothalamus.
source: Thus, the central effects of acute HFD are distinct from those of chronic HFD, and have little to no effect on microglial expansion, transcription, heterogeneity, or inflammation in the hypothalamus.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing no changes in these parameters.

claim: Cellular metabolic changes are necessary and sufficient mediators of cell-type-specific function.
source: A deep body of literature has highlighted how cellular metabolic changes are necessary and sufficient mediators of cell-type-specific function, work revitalised of late by the immunometabolism community (Pearce et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential was increased in primary MBH microglia sorted from animals administered a 3d HFD.
source: Interestingly, mitochondrial membrane potential was increased in primary MBH microglia sorted from animals administered a 3d HFD (MitoTracker Deep Red; Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures using MitoTracker staining.

claim: Co-staining showed no evidence of altered mitochondrial mass upon 3d HFD.
source: Co-staining in the same samples showed no evidence of altered mitochondrial mass (MitoTracker Green; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: aMMR was detectable within 12 hr of high-fat feeding.
source: This aMMR was detectable within 12 hr of high-fat feeding (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: aMMR appeared transient and distinct from chronic HFD response; parallel measures showed no induction of membrane potential in 4-week HFD animals.
source: Importantly, aMMR appeared transient and distinct from chronic HFD response; parallel measures showed no induction of membrane potential in 4-week HFD animals (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Microglia respond to acute HFD with a unique and specific acute mitochondrial metabolic response.
source: Thus, microglia respond to acute HFD with a unique and specific acute mitochondrial metabolic response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mitochondrial membrane potential data.

claim: Relatively few metabolites change in CSF upon 3d HFD.
source: Overall, relatively few metabolites change upon 3d HFD.
evidence: This is supported by CSF metabolomics data.

claim: Nicotinamide-N-oxide was the only metabolite that decreased significantly in CSF upon 3d HFD.
source: Nicotinamide-N-oxide was the only metabolite that decreased significantly; and six metabolites increased upon 3d HFD including methylmalonate, isovalerylcarnitine, nicotinic acid, glutarylcarnitine, and the fatty acids, palmitate (hexadecanoic acid) and stearate (octadecanoic acid).
evidence: This is supported by CSF metabolomics data.

claim: Six metabolites increased in CSF upon 3d HFD including methylmalonate, isovalerylcarnitine, nicotinic acid, glutarylcarnitine, palmitate, and stearate.
source: Nicotinamide-N-oxide was the only metabolite that decreased significantly; and six metabolites increased upon 3d HFD including methylmalonate, isovalerylcarnitine, nicotinic acid, glutarylcarnitine, and the fatty acids, palmitate (hexadecanoic acid) and stearate (octadecanoic acid).
evidence: This is supported by CSF metabolomics data.

claim: Palmitate and stearate are highly enriched in the HFD itself (Research Diets D12492).
source: Palmitate and stearate, the only two metabolites that changed by >2-fold, are highly enriched in the HFD itself (Research Diets D12492) suggesting that microglia respond 'directly' to dietary fatty acid levels.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the diet composition.

claim: Microglia respond 'directly' to dietary fatty acid levels.
source: Palmitate and stearate, the only two metabolites that changed by >2-fold, are highly enriched in the HFD itself (Research Diets D12492) suggesting that microglia respond 'directly' to dietary fatty acid levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CSF metabolomics data and diet composition.

claim: Palmitate had no effect on either baseline or maximal oxygen consumption under standard culture conditions.
source: Palmitate had no effect on either baseline or maximal oxygen consumption under standard culture conditions (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse experimental data shown in figures.

claim: When added in conjunction with succinate, palmitate-treated microglia were unable to utilize succinate.
source: That said, when added in conjunction with succinate (to prime complex II-mediated OxPhos), palmitate-treated microglia were unable to utilize succinate.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse experimental data.

claim: Acute palmitate rapidly compromises or saturates complex II function and prevents utilization of substrates routed through complex II.
source: Acute palmitate therefore appears to rapidly compromise or saturate complex II function and prevent utilization of substrates routed through complex II.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Seahorse data showing inability to use succinate.

claim: Fresh primary microglia from 3d HFD animals failed to respond to complex II-specific mitochondrial stimuli.
source: Consistent with these in vitro findings, fresh primary microglia from 3d HFD animals failed to respond to complex II-specific mitochondrial stimuli (rotenone+succinate; Figure 2F) validating the findings in adult, ex vivo contexts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures using TMRM staining.

claim: In vitro palmitate exposure decreased microglial mitochondrial length within 24 hr.
source: Consistent with the in vivo observations above, in vitro palmitate exposure decreased microglial mitochondrial length within 24 hr, indicating that fatty acid exposure itself is sufficient to trigger mitochondrial fission in a cell autonomous manner (Figure 2G, upper panels).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures using MitoTracker staining.

claim: Fatty acid exposure is sufficient to trigger mitochondrial fission in microglia in a cell autonomous manner.
source: Consistent with the in vivo observations above, in vitro palmitate exposure decreased microglial mitochondrial length within 24 hr, indicating that fatty acid exposure itself is sufficient to trigger mitochondrial fission in a cell autonomous manner (Figure 2G, upper panels).
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vitro palmitate exposure data.

claim: Kim et al. observed mitochondrial fission and DRP1 phosphorylation upon 3d HFD-treated mice.
source: This result also confirms observations by Kim et al. who observed mitochondrial fission and DRP1 phosphorylation upon 3d HFD-treated mice (Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The microglial responses to palmitate were independent of any mitoSOX-detectable ROS release.
source: Collectively, these responses were independent of any mitoSOX-detectable ROS release (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and were associated with recruitment of the mitochondrial fission regulator DRP1 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Palmitate exposure was associated with recruitment of the mitochondrial fission regulator DRP1.
source: Collectively, these responses were independent of any mitoSOX-detectable ROS release (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and were associated with recruitment of the mitochondrial fission regulator DRP1 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures using DRP1 immunostaining.

claim: A 24 hr exposure to the mono-unsaturated fatty acid oleate failed to elicit a comparable fission response.
source: A 24 hr exposure to the mono-unsaturated fatty acid oleate failed to elicit a comparable fission response (Figure 2G), and, acute palmitate exposure had no effects on microglial cytokine release in vitro (IL6, IL1β, TNFα; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Acute palmitate exposure had no effects on microglial cytokine release in vitro (IL6, IL1β, TNFα).
source: A 24 hr exposure to the mono-unsaturated fatty acid oleate failed to elicit a comparable fission response (Figure 2G), and, acute palmitate exposure had no effects on microglial cytokine release in vitro (IL6, IL1β, TNFα; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures measuring cytokine concentrations.

claim: Acute in vitro fatty acid exposure recapitulates in vivo aMMR, including selective loss of complex II activity and lack of significant inflammatory cytokine response.
source: Thus, acute in vitro fatty acid exposure recapitulates in vivo aMMR, including selective loss of complex II activity and lack of significant inflammatory cytokine response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: Drp1MGKO animals were born at Mendelian ratios and grow normally.
source: Drp1MGKO animals were born at Mendelian ratios and grow normally.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from breeding experiments.

claim: Tamoxifen injection followed by 4 weeks washout generated the intended Drp1 deletion.
source: Tamoxifen injection followed by 4 weeks washout generated the intended Drp1 deletion (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Wakabayashi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and cited literature.

claim: Body weight, fat mass, and lean mass regulation were normal in Drp1MGKO mice both before and after tamoxifen injection.
source: Body weight, fat mass, and lean mass regulation were normal both before and after tamoxifen injection in Drp1MGKO mice, indicating that microglial DRP1 (and by extension microglial mitochondrial fusion) is dispensable for body weight regulation under standard conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Microglial DRP1 is dispensable for body weight regulation under standard conditions.
source: Body weight, fat mass, and lean mass regulation were normal both before and after tamoxifen injection in Drp1MGKO mice, indicating that microglial DRP1 (and by extension microglial mitochondrial fusion) is dispensable for body weight regulation under standard conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the body weight data in Drp1MGKO mice.

claim: Microglial mitochondrial fusion is dispensable for body weight regulation under standard conditions.
source: Body weight, fat mass, and lean mass regulation were normal both before and after tamoxifen injection in Drp1MGKO mice, indicating that microglial DRP1 (and by extension microglial mitochondrial fusion) is dispensable for body weight regulation under standard conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of DRP1 in mitochondrial fission and the body weight data.

claim: The finding that microglial DRP1 is dispensable for baseline body weight regulation is consistent with literature.
source: These data are consistent with literature (Gao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Drp1MGKO mice showed normal glucose and insulin tolerance.
source: Drp1MGKO mice also showed normal glucose and insulin tolerance (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: 3d HFD triggered post-absorptive hyperglycemia and enhanced glucose-induced insulin release in control animals.
source: Importantly, whereas 3d HFD triggered post-absorptive hyperglycemia and enhanced glucose-induced insulin release in control animals, Drp1MGKO failed to mount a comparable whole-body metabolic response (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Drp1MGKO mice failed to mount a comparable whole-body metabolic response to 3d HFD.
source: Importantly, whereas 3d HFD triggered post-absorptive hyperglycemia and enhanced glucose-induced insulin release in control animals, Drp1MGKO failed to mount a comparable whole-body metabolic response (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Microglial mitochondrial dynamics are dispensable for baseline control of body weight and glucose homeostasis.
source: Thus, while microglial mitochondrial dynamics are dispensable for baseline control of body weight and glucose homeostasis, they are absolutely necessary for the very earliest metabolic anomalies induced when switching to HFD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Drp1MGKO experimental data.

claim: Microglial mitochondrial dynamics are absolutely necessary for the very earliest metabolic anomalies induced when switching to HFD.
source: Thus, while microglial mitochondrial dynamics are dispensable for baseline control of body weight and glucose homeostasis, they are absolutely necessary for the very earliest metabolic anomalies induced when switching to HFD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Drp1MGKO experimental data.

claim: The 3d HFD-induced hyperglycemia observed under overtly catabolic conditions is microglia independent.
source: Consistent with the data from Figure 1, the 3d HFD-induced hyperglycemia that is observed under overtly catabolic conditions, which we found to be microglia independent (Figure 1C), was still present in Drp1MGKO animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The metabolic responses to acute HFD are highly specific and include both microglia-dependent and independent mechanisms.
source: These data reinforce the conclusion that the metabolic responses to acute HFD are highly specific and include both microglia-dependent and independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined experimental data from PLX5622 and Drp1MGKO experiments.

claim: Microglial mitochondrial dynamics are required for the immediate in vivo homeostatic response to 3d HFD.
source: Thus, microglial mitochondrial dynamics are required for the immediate in vivo homeostatic response to 3d HFD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Drp1MGKO experimental data.

claim: Metabolite tracing experiments on primary adult microglia are not currently feasible due to long isolation times.
source: Due in part to the long isolation times required to generate pure primary adult microglia, metabolite tracing experiments on primary adult microglia are not currently feasible.
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations.

claim: Primary murine neonatal microglia were chosen as the model for mechanistic experiments.
source: We therefore chose primary murine neonatal microglia as our model of choice for more mechanistic experiments (Valdearcos et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and is supported by citation.

claim: Primary microglia increase lipid droplet numbers within 24 hr of in vitro exposure to palmitate.
source: Using BODIPY fluorescence as a readout, we found that primary microglia increase lipid droplet numbers within 24 hr of in vitro exposure to palmitate (200 µM; Figure 4A), demonstrating a capacity to take up fatty acids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures using BODIPY staining.

claim: Primary microglia have a capacity to take up fatty acids.
source: Using BODIPY fluorescence as a readout, we found that primary microglia increase lipid droplet numbers within 24 hr of in vitro exposure to palmitate (200 µM; Figure 4A), demonstrating a capacity to take up fatty acids.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lipid droplet accumulation data.

claim: Primary microglia incubated with 13C-palmitate showed significant palmitate uptake and incorporation into downstream metabolites.
source: Focusing first on the control microglia we observed significant palmitate uptake and incorporation into downstream metabolites (Figure 4C–F, O and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing experimental data shown in figures and tables.

claim: This is the first definitive demonstration that microglia metabolize fatty acids.
source: This is the first definitive demonstration to our knowledge that microglia metabolize fatty acids.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: 13C-palmitate label was processed to palmitoylcarnitine and acetylcarnitine indicating that microglial fatty acid metabolism acts via the canonical CPT1/CPT2 pathway.
source: 13C-palmitate label was processed to palmitoylcarnitine and acetylcarnitine indicating that microglial fatty acid metabolism acts via the canonical CPT1/CPT2 pathway, moving carbons from outside the mitochondria into the inner mitochondrial matrix (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the 13C-tracing data and knowledge of fatty acid metabolism pathways.

claim: 13C-labeling was found in 13C-acetylserine, indicating that palmitate is processed through β-oxidation and contributes to the acetyl-coA pool.
source: 13C-labeling was also found in 13C-acetylserine, indicating that palmitate is processed through β-oxidation and that it contributes to the acetyl-coA pool (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the 13C-tracing data and knowledge of metabolism.

claim: Label was detected in all measured TCA cycle intermediates.
source: Label was detected in all measured TCA cycle intermediates (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The labeling ratios of TCA intermediates and glutamate indicated that microglia push a substantial fraction of palmitate-derived carbons out of the TCA toward glutamate rather than processing them further through the whole TCA cycle.
source: The labeling ratios of TCA intermediates and glutamate indicated that microglia push a substantial fraction of palmitate-derived carbons out of the TCA (alpha-ketoglutarate [a-KG] to glutamate) rather than processing them further through the whole TCA cycle (toward malate) (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the 13C-tracing data showing labeling patterns.

claim: Microglia store and metabolize palmitate toward energy and toward a unique set of anaplerotic reactions.
source: Thus, microglia store and metabolize palmitate toward energy and toward a unique set of anaplerotic reactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined 13C-tracing data.

claim: Under control conditions, microglia exhibited strong glucose uptake, glycolysis, and incorporation of glucose label into TCA intermediates.
source: Under control conditions, microglia exhibited strong glucose uptake, glycolysis, and incorporation of glucose label into TCA intermediates (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Substantial 13C labeling from glucose was detected in pyruvate, citrate, a-KG, malate, and glutamate.
source: Substantial 13C labeling was detected in pyruvate, citrate, a-KG, malate, and again in glutamate.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing experimental data.

claim: The TCA shunt toward glutamate/glutamine pathway is a unique characteristic of the microglial metabolic fingerprint and not specific to palmitate routing.
source: These data confirm that the unexpected TCA shunt toward glutamate/glutamine pathway is a unique characteristic of the microglial metabolic fingerprint and not specific to palmitate routing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of similar glutamate production with both palmitate and glucose tracers.

claim: 13C-glucose-derived metabolites were detected extracellularly in the form of glutamate, itaconate, succinate, and lactate.
source: Importantly, 13C-glucose-derived metabolites were also detected extracellularly in the form of glutamate, itaconate, and succinate, as well as in extracellular lactate (m+3) (Figure 4K–N).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing experimental data measuring extracellular metabolites.

claim: Palmitate pretreatment increased glucose uptake.
source: And, palmitate pretreatment increased all of these signatures, including glucose uptake (Figure 4J), lactate labeling, and lactate release.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Palmitate pretreatment increased lactate labeling and lactate release.
source: And, palmitate pretreatment increased all of these signatures, including glucose uptake (Figure 4J), lactate labeling, and lactate release.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing experimental data.

claim: Fatty acid pretreatment increased release of tracer-labeled itaconate and succinate into the extracellular media.
source: Interestingly, as with palmitate-tracing experiments, fatty acid pretreatment increased release of tracer-labeled taconite and succinate into the extracellular media (Figure 4L–M).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing experimental data shown in figures.

claim: aMMR is characterized by synergistic induction of a Warburg-like metabolic signature by glucose and palmitate.
source: aMMR is therefore characterized by synergistic induction of a Warburg-like metabolic signature by glucose and palmitate, and significant release of carbon fuels to the cell exterior (Figure 4N).
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined 13C-tracing data showing increased glycolysis and lactate release.

claim: aMMR is characterized by significant release of carbon fuels to the cell exterior.
source: aMMR is therefore characterized by synergistic induction of a Warburg-like metabolic signature by glucose and palmitate, and significant release of carbon fuels to the cell exterior (Figure 4N).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing data showing extracellular labeled metabolites.

claim: Microglia are a novel metabolic and neuroprotective node, able to take up harmful free fatty acids and repurpose them to fuel surrounding cells in the form of lactate and anaplerotic substrates.
source: Collectively, these data identify microglia as a novel metabolic and neuroprotective node, able to take up harmful free fatty acids and repurpose them to fuel surrounding cells in the form of lactate and anaplerotic substrates (Figure 4O).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined experimental data.

claim: Changes in neuronal function have previously been linked to lactate provided by astrocytes.
source: Changes in neuronal function have previously been linked to lactate provided by astrocytes (Pellerin, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Neurons treated with microglial conditioned media showed substantial m+3 lactate at levels that far exceeded labeling triggered by glucose tracer alone.
source: Intriguingly, and consistent with literature documenting poor direct glucose utilization by neurons (Bouzier-Sore et al., 2006), we found substantial m+3 lactate (as well as other metabolites) in neurons treated with microglial conditioned media, and at levels that far exceeded labeling triggered by glucose tracer alone (Figure 5A, middle column vs left column) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing experimental data on neurons shown in figures and cited literature.

claim: The data indicate higher uptake of citrate and itaconate from the control microglia-conditioned media.
source: The data indicate higher uptake of citrate and itaconate from the control microglia-conditioned media, further supporting the hypothesis that neuronal metabolism is reproducibly impacted by palmitate-triggered changes in microglial products.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data measuring labeled metabolites in neurons.

claim: Neuronal metabolism is reproducibly impacted by palmitate-triggered changes in microglial products.
source: The data indicate higher uptake of citrate and itaconate from the control microglia-conditioned media, further supporting the hypothesis that neuronal metabolism is reproducibly impacted by palmitate-triggered changes in microglial products.
evidence: This is an inference based on the neuronal uptake data of microglial-derived metabolites.

claim: Palmitate metabolism by microglia modulates neuronal carbon substrate use in vitro.
source: These data demonstrate that palmitate metabolism by microglia modulates neuronal carbon substrate use in vitro, and, they highlight the relative importance of this process compared to uptake of pure glucose.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conditioned media experiments.

claim: The data highlight the relative importance of microglial metabolite provision compared to direct neuronal uptake of pure glucose.
source: These data demonstrate that palmitate metabolism by microglia modulates neuronal carbon substrate use in vitro, and, they highlight the relative importance of this process compared to uptake of pure glucose.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of neuronal labeling from conditioned media vs direct glucose.

claim: aMMR may alter neuronal function in vivo through a candidate mechanism involving microglial metabolite release.
source: The data identify a candidate mechanism by which aMMR may alter neuronal function in vivo.
evidence: This is speculation based on the in vitro data showing neuronal uptake of microglial-derived metabolites.

claim: 3d HFD exposure triggered an increase in mitochondrial membrane potential in cortical microglia.
source: Indeed, 3d HFD exposure triggered an increase in mitochondrial membrane potential in both cortical and hippocampal microglia (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: 3d HFD exposure triggered an increase in mitochondrial membrane potential in hippocampal microglia.
source: Indeed, 3d HFD exposure triggered an increase in mitochondrial membrane potential in both cortical and hippocampal microglia (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The cortical and hippocampal microglial data were consistent with the CSF results.
source: These data were consistent with the CSF results and suggested therefore that acute high-fat feeding might alter higher cognitive function.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the CSF metabolomics to the brain-wide microglial response.

claim: Acute high-fat feeding might alter higher cognitive function.
source: These data were consistent with the CSF results and suggested therefore that acute high-fat feeding might alter higher cognitive function.
evidence: This is speculation based on the hippocampal microglial response.

claim: 3d HFD mice exhibited a faster reaction in the Barnes Test suggestive of improved learning and spatial memory.
source: Using a standard Barnes Test, 3d HFD mice exhibited a faster reaction (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) suggestive of improved learning and spatial memory.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in figures.

claim: 3d HFD exposed animals exhibited heightened spatial memory in the T-Maze.
source: Similarly, when challenged with a T-Maze, 3d HFD exposed animals exhibited heightened spatial memory (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in figures.

claim: The memory phenotypes were reproducible at two different institutes (VAI, USA, and MPI-IE, Germany) and in the hands of different experimentalists.
source: These phenotypes were reproducible at two different institutes (VAI, USA, and MPI-IE, Germany) and in the hands of different experimentalists (Figure 5D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data from multiple locations shown in figures.

claim: The memory differences were observed in the absence of any detectable changes to motor coordination.
source: Notably, the memory differences were observed in the absence of any detectable changes to motor coordination (ROTAROD; Figure 5F–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by ROTAROD test data shown in figures.

claim: PLX-5622-treated animals failed to show any detectable memory improvements upon a 3d HFD.
source: Importantly, PLX-5622-treated animals failed to show any detectable memory improvements upon a 3d HFD (Figure 5I and J, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C) indicating indeed that an intact microglial compartment is necessary for acute HFD enhancement of memory function.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data in microglial-depleted mice shown in figures.

claim: An intact microglial compartment is necessary for acute HFD enhancement of memory function.
source: Importantly, PLX-5622-treated animals failed to show any detectable memory improvements upon a 3d HFD (Figure 5I and J, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C) indicating indeed that an intact microglial compartment is necessary for acute HFD enhancement of memory function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PLX5622 behavioral test data.

claim: 3d HFD exposure failed to trigger memory improvements in Drp1MGKO mice.
source: Likewise, 3d HFD exposure failed to trigger memory improvements in Drp1MGKO mice (Figure 5K, Figure 5—figure supplement 2D) indicating that the memory enhancing response, like the glucose homeostatic effect, is microglial DRP1-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data in Drp1MGKO mice shown in figures.

claim: The memory enhancing response to 3d HFD is microglial DRP1-dependent.
source: Likewise, 3d HFD exposure failed to trigger memory improvements in Drp1MGKO mice (Figure 5K, Figure 5—figure supplement 2D) indicating that the memory enhancing response, like the glucose homeostatic effect, is microglial DRP1-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Drp1MGKO behavioral test data.

claim: No mice in any treatment group showed altered motor effects by ROTAROD.
source: Again, no mice in any treatment group showed altered motor effects by ROTAROD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–J and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by ROTAROD test data shown in figures.

claim: The aMMR in response to 3d HFD constitutes a generalized response that couples acute dietary changes to diverse central functions.
source: Therefore, the aMMR in response to 3d HFD constitutes a generalized response that couples acute dietary changes to diverse central functions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined data showing effects on both metabolism and memory.

claim: The data identify a new role for microglial cells as a rapid metabolic sensor of dietary macronutrient composition.
source: Our data identify a new role for microglial cells as a rapid metabolic sensor of dietary macronutrient composition, and as a relay that triggers cognitive and peripheral metabolic responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined experimental data.

claim: Microglial cells act as a relay that triggers cognitive and peripheral metabolic responses.
source: Our data identify a new role for microglial cells as a rapid metabolic sensor of dietary macronutrient composition, and as a relay that triggers cognitive and peripheral metabolic responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined experimental data.

claim: Chronic HFD causes adverse outcomes in both the brain (microgliosis, inflammatory cytokine release, myeloid cell infiltration) and periphery (hyperglycemia, insulin resistance).
source: Whereas a bulk of literature demonstrates adverse outcomes upon chronic HFD, both in the brain (microgliosis, inflammatory cytokine release, myeloid cell infiltration) and periphery (hyperglycemia, insulin resistance) (Thaler et al., 2012; Valdearcos et al., 2017), our findings indicate that acute HFD initiates a distinct homeostatic response that supports cognitive function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Acute HFD initiates a distinct homeostatic response that supports cognitive function.
source: Whereas a bulk of literature demonstrates adverse outcomes upon chronic HFD, both in the brain (microgliosis, inflammatory cytokine release, myeloid cell infiltration) and periphery (hyperglycemia, insulin resistance) (Thaler et al., 2012; Valdearcos et al., 2017), our findings indicate that acute HFD initiates a distinct homeostatic response that supports cognitive function.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing memory improvements.

claim: There are obvious evolutionary benefits to partitioning energy use toward cognition when energy needs are met.
source: Evolutionarily, there are obvious benefits to partitioning energy use toward cognition when energy needs are met.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary advantages.

claim: aMMR could result from direct uptake, processing, and release of fatty acid-derived carbons.
source: We propose that aMMR could result from direct uptake, processing, and release of fatty acid-derived carbons, and demonstrate that microglia are capable of metabolizing fatty acids toward diverse intracellular and extracellular pools.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: Microglia are capable of metabolizing fatty acids toward diverse intracellular and extracellular pools.
source: We propose that aMMR could result from direct uptake, processing, and release of fatty acid-derived carbons, and demonstrate that microglia are capable of metabolizing fatty acids toward diverse intracellular and extracellular pools.
evidence: This is supported by the 13C-tracing experimental data.

claim: One possibility is that the response requires flexibility between lipid storage and processing, and that this becomes saturated with prolonged HFD.
source: One possibility is that the response requires flexibility between lipid storage and processing, and that this becomes saturated with prolonged HFD.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of transition from acute to chronic HFD effects.

claim: Microglial ablation has no overt effect on baseline metabolism and memory.
source: Of equal interest are the PLX5622 experiments and data, which demonstrate for the first time that microglial ablation has no overt effect on baseline metabolism and memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from PLX5622-treated mice.

claim: Microglia are critical for optimal response to dietary change.
source: Importantly, however, the data show that microglia are critical for optimal response to dietary change.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PLX5622 and Drp1MGKO experimental data.

claim: CSFR1 inhibiting compounds such as PLX5622 deplete not only microglia but also long living CNS macrophages in the meninges and perivascular space.
source: We are aware of the fact that CSFR1 inhibiting compounds such as PLX5622 deplete not only microglia but also long living CNS macrophages in the meninges and perivascular space (Goldmann et al., 2016) but they are by far less numerous and placed far from neurons in the parenchyma.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and acknowledges a limitation of the PLX5622 approach.

claim: CNS macrophages in the meninges and perivascular space are by far less numerous than microglia and placed far from neurons in the parenchyma.
source: We are aware of the fact that CSFR1 inhibiting compounds such as PLX5622 deplete not only microglia but also long living CNS macrophages in the meninges and perivascular space (Goldmann et al., 2016) but they are by far less numerous and placed far from neurons in the parenchyma.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about CNS cell populations.

claim: Microglia mediate a glucose-sparing function during the transition from post-prandial to fasted states.
source: We demonstrate a novel role for microglia in optimizing glycemia upon short- (2 hr) but not long- (24 hr) term fasting and therefore suggest that microglia mediate a glucose-sparing function during the transition from post-prandial to fasted states.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential effects of microglial depletion on 2 hr vs overnight fasting glycemia.

claim: The overabundance of food since industrialization has skewed a significant global population toward chronic prandial and post-prandial states and away from intermittent fast-feed cycles.
source: The overabundance of food since industrialization has skewed a significant global population toward chronic prandial and post-prandial states and away from intermittent fast-feed cycles.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about modern dietary patterns.

claim: aMMR coordinates central metabolic balance with peripheral glucose homeostasis selectively during the prandial/post-prandial phase.
source: The finding that aMMR coordinates central metabolic balance with peripheral glucose homeostasis selectively during the prandial/post-prandial phase adds nuance to a significant literature distinguishing these physiological contexts (Dakic et al., 2017; Havel, 2001; Zeltser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: From an evolutionary perspective it is easy to rationalize why initial periods of plenty would be mechanistically coupled to maximizing central functions.
source: From an evolutionary perspective it is easy to rationalize why initial periods of plenty would be mechanistically coupled to maximizing central functions.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary advantages.

claim: Microglia provide several TCA-associated substrates into the extracellular milieu.
source: Our data indicate that microglia provide several TCA-associated substrates into the extracellular milieu, and, that palmitate/HFD increases this activity.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing data showing extracellular metabolites.

claim: Palmitate/HFD increases microglial release of TCA-associated substrates into the extracellular milieu.
source: Our data indicate that microglia provide several TCA-associated substrates into the extracellular milieu, and, that palmitate/HFD increases this activity.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing data comparing BSA vs palmitate conditions.

claim: Tanycytes and astrocytes have both been documented to release select metabolites into the extracellular environment.
source: Tanycytes and astrocytes have both been documented to release select metabolites into the extracellular environment (García-Cáceres et al., 2019; Barca-Mayo and López, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The experiments do not completely rule out a contribution of other cell types in coupling acute HFD intake to memory and learning.
source: The experiments presented here do not completely rule out a contribution of these or cell types in coupling acute HFD intake to memory and learning.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: A cooperative model is suspected over hierarchical, serial, or synergistic metabolic compartmentalization models for glial-neuronal metabolic interactions.
source: Given that CSF production is only loosely compartmentalized (e.g. relative to the highly physically structured control of blood), we suspect a cooperative model over hierarchical, serial, or synergistic metabolic compartmentalization models.
evidence: This is speculation about the organization of metabolic interactions.

claim: aMMR involves release of at least four important anapleurotic substrates.
source: Here, we demonstrate that aMMR involves release of at least four important anapleurotic substrates, and that aMMR is detectable from the hypothalamus to the hippocampus and cortex.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing data showing extracellular lactate, glutamate, succinate, and itaconate.

claim: Increased lactate has been shown to enhance fear memory in a glutamate-associated mechanism.
source: Increased lactate has been shown to enhance fear memory in a glutamate-associated mechanism (Ikeda et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Both lactate and glutamate are increased upon 3d HFD.
source: Both lactate and glutamate are increased upon 3d HFD suggesting that aMMR may comprise a much more complex behavioral response.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing experimental data.

claim: aMMR may comprise a much more complex behavioral response.
source: Both lactate and glutamate are increased upon 3d HFD suggesting that aMMR may comprise a much more complex behavioral response.
evidence: This is speculation based on the metabolite data and cited literature.

claim: The data demonstrate that mitochondrial fission is necessary for aMMR.
source: In addition to identifying novel substrate routing patterns in microglia, our data demonstrate that mitochondrial fission is necessary for aMMR.
evidence: This is supported by the Drp1MGKO experimental data.

claim: Fatty acid-triggered fission has been observed in several cell types including neurons and glial cells.
source: Fatty acid-triggered fission has been observed in several cell types (Buck et al., 2016) including neurons and glial cells (Schneeberger et al., 2013; Ramírez et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Work by Kim et al., 2019, suggests that the aMMR characterized here may require UCP2.
source: Work by Kim et al., 2019, suggests that the aMMR characterized here may require UCP2; those authors demonstrated UCP2-dependent mitochondrial changes in short- and long-term HFD exposed hypothalamic microglia.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The two studies (current and Kim et al.) collectively argue against astrocytes being the only cells able to use fatty acids and release fatty acid-derived substrates for use by neurons and neighboring cells.
source: Collectively, the two studies argue against astrocytes being the only cells in their ability to use fatty acids and release fatty acid-derived substrates for use by neurons and neighboring cells (Westergaard et al., 1995).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current data and cited literature.

claim: Studies have identified stearate and palmitate in the CSF of patients with chronic obesity and with diabetes.
source: Studies have identified stearate and palmitate in the CSF of patients with chronic obesity and with diabetes, reports that highlight the importance of these findings (Melo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: This study demonstrates unappreciated plasticity and complexity in microglial cellular metabolism.
source: Finally, this study demonstrates unappreciated plasticity and complexity in microglial cellular metabolism.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined experimental data.

claim: Primary microglia from across the brain readily take up, metabolize, and store fatty acids.
source: Rather than being glucose-constrained, we reveal that primary microglia from across the brain readily take up, metabolize, and store fatty acids and that fatty acids are metabolized toward bioenergetic and acetylation reactions (acetyl-coA).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-palmitate tracing and BODIPY staining data.

claim: Fatty acids are metabolized toward bioenergetic and acetylation reactions (acetyl-coA) in microglia.
source: Rather than being glucose-constrained, we reveal that primary microglia from across the brain readily take up, metabolize, and store fatty acids and that fatty acids are metabolized toward bioenergetic and acetylation reactions (acetyl-coA).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-palmitate tracing data showing labeled acetylcarnitine and acetylserine.

claim: This is the first proof that substantial β-oxidation occurs in microglial cells even in the presence of high extracellular glucose.
source: They prove for the first time that substantial β-oxidation occurs in microglial cells even in the presence of high extracellular glucose (Kalsbeek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on the 13C-palmitate tracing data and cited literature.

claim: Palmitate metabolism drives feedforward inhibition of complex II via itaconate production.
source: The coordinate observations of intra- and extracellular succinate, itaconate accumulation, and relative complex II inhibition indicate that palmitate metabolism drives feedforward inhibition of complex II via itaconate production and shunting of TCA intermediates out of the cycle toward glutamate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data showing itaconate production, complex II inhibition, and glutamate accumulation.

claim: Palmitate metabolism drives shunting of TCA intermediates out of the cycle toward glutamate.
source: The coordinate observations of intra- and extracellular succinate, itaconate accumulation, and relative complex II inhibition indicate that palmitate metabolism drives feedforward inhibition of complex II via itaconate production and shunting of TCA intermediates out of the cycle toward glutamate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the 13C-tracing data showing labeling patterns.

claim: Further examination of the role of glutamine as a fuel and anapleurotic regulator of cellular function is warranted.
source: Further examination of the role of glutamine as a fuel and anapleurotic regulator of cellular function is therefore warranted.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research based on the findings.

claim: Under standard conditions, microglia appear metabolically wired to release lactate, succinate, glutamate, citrate, and itaconate.
source: At least under the standard conditions used here, microglia appear metabolically wired to also release lactate, succinate, glutamate, citrate, and itaconate.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-tracing data showing these metabolites in extracellular media.

claim: The lack of substantial intracellular lipid accumulation, respiration, or ROS buildup upon prolonged palmitate exposure is consistent with substrate release.
source: The idea is consistent with the observed lack of substantial intracellular lipid accumulation, respiration, or ROS buildup upon prolonged palmitate exposure.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the metabolite release to the lack of intracellular accumulation.

claim: Substrate release could mediate the learning and memory effects that accompany aMMR.
source: Such substrate release could mediate the learning and memory effects that accompany aMMR; they are consistent with the data of other studies that have examined metabolite associations with learning and memory (Morgunov et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2023; Serra et al., 2022; Cline et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior literature on metabolites and memory.
